title: Pakistan's Sikhs
hook: Sikhs still live in Nankana Sahib, Peshawar and other towns

segments.voice: Yesterday, Afghanistan's Sikhs, and your line was a small community. Did you show up for a small group? Today, Sikhs who live on the far side of a line on the map. Day one thousand thirty.

On the Indian side of the border, near the town of Dera Baba Nanak, there's a raised platform where pilgrims have stood with binoculars. They are looking across fields at a white gurdwara on the other side: Kartarpur Sahib, where tradition says Guru Nanak spent his last years farming and singing. For a long time, that look through glass was as close as many could get. Then a corridor opened that let pilgrims from India cross for the day, though it has been shut again in tense times. When they do cross, they find something the binoculars never showed: Sikhs who live there, and never left.
screen: `BINOCULARS AT THE BORDER.` → `KARTARPUR SAHIB ACROSS THE FIELDS.` → `SIKHS WHO NEVER LEFT.`

segments.voice: First, the line. When Partition divided Punjab, a border ran through the Sikh homeland, and families on both sides were uprooted in great suffering. Sikh families from the western side moved east. But the places didn't move. Second, the places. Tradition says Guru Nanak was born at Talwandi, now called Nankana Sahib. Kartarpur Sahib is where he settled. Panja Sahib holds the story of the hand on the rock. In Lahore, Gurdwara Dera Sahib marks where tradition says Guru Arjan was martyred. Much of the Sikh story's early map now lies across the border. Third, the people who stayed. Sikh families still live in Nankana Sahib, in Peshawar, and in other towns. They run shops, go to school, sit in the gurdwara, and on the great days they host pilgrims who cross from India and arrive from everywhere else. For a few days the sangat is enormous; then it is small again, and the local families keep the lamps lit. Fourth, the old song. In a hymn of Guru Arjan, at Ang 611 of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru says there is one father, and we are all the children of the one. A border can decide which passport you carry. It can't decide whose child you are. That is today's line: across the border. One family of the Guru, on two sides of a line.
screen: `PARTITION DREW A LINE.` · `NANKANA, KARTARPUR, PANJA, DERA SAHIB.` · `FAMILIES WHO STAYED.` · `ANG 611: ONE FATHER, ONE FAMILY.` · then, large: `ACROSS THE BORDER.`

segments.voice: Two minutes across a border. Sit, and let your eyes close or soften. Picture a line on a map, any line you know, between countries, cities, or two sides of a family. Now picture people on the far side of it going about an ordinary morning. Opening a shop. Walking a child to school. Sitting in a gurdwara before work. Breathe in, and see them. Breathe out, and let the line fade a little. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out, for those on both sides. The bell holds the time.
Pakistan's Sikhs. Families who still live in Nankana Sahib, Peshawar and other towns, keeping the Guru's places alive and welcoming pilgrims. Today's word.
Your line: across the border. Today, think of someone on the other side of a line in your own life, and send them one friendly word. Day one thousand thirty.

howItsDone: Sikhs in Pakistan keep gurdwaras in Nankana Sahib, Peshawar and other towns, and on gurpurabs they host pilgrims from India and other countries; when it is open, the Kartarpur corridor lets pilgrims from India visit Kartarpur Sahib for the day.
